sections.section_title: The Spirit Commissions the First Deliberate Mission
sections.summary: During worship and fasting at Antioch, the Holy Spirit commands the community to set apart Barnabas and Saul for the work to which he has already called them; the church lays hands on them and sends them off.

sections.section_title: The Mission Begins in the Synagogues
sections.summary: Sent out by the Holy Spirit, Barnabas and Saul sail to Cyprus and proclaim the word of God in the synagogues at Salamis, with John Mark assisting.

sections.section_title: A Jewish False Prophet, a Gentile Proconsul, and the Name Paul
sections.summary: At Paphos, the Jewish magician Bar-Jesus opposes the missionaries and tries to turn the proconsul Sergius Paulus from the faith; Paul, filled with the Holy Spirit, pronounces temporary blindness on Bar-Jesus, and the proconsul believes.

sections.section_title: Pisidian Antioch -- An Invitation to Speak
sections.summary: Paul and companions travel to Pisidian Antioch, where they enter the synagogue on the Sabbath and are invited by the rulers to give a word of encouragement; John Mark departs and returns to Jerusalem.

Paul addresses the synagogue audience (both 'men of Israel' and God-fearers) with a historical review in which God is the subject of every verb: God chose the fathers, made the people great in Egypt, led them out, endured the wilderness, gave the land, provided judges, gave Saul as king, then raised up David as a man after God's own heart.

Paul declares that from David's offspring God has brought to Israel a Savior, Jesus, as promised, with John the Baptist serving as the forerunner who pointed beyond himself to the one coming after him.

Paul addresses both Jews and God-fearers as recipients of the salvation message, then declares that Jerusalem's rulers, by failing to recognize Jesus and condemning him, ironically fulfilled the very prophetic scriptures they read every Sabbath.

Paul argues that God raised Jesus from the dead, proving it from Psalm 2:7 (enthronement as God's Son), Isaiah 55:3 (the sure blessings of David requiring a living recipient), and Psalm 16:10 (God's Holy One will not see corruption) -- David himself died and decayed, so the psalm must refer to Jesus whom God raised.

sections.section_title: Forgiveness Beyond the Law, and a Warning
sections.summary: Paul declares that through Jesus forgiveness of sins is proclaimed and that 'everyone who believes is freed from everything from which you could not be freed by the law of Moses,' then warns with Habakkuk 1:5 that God is doing an unbelievable work and the hearers must not be among those who refuse to believe it.

sections.section_title: The Initial Response -- Urged to Continue in Grace
sections.summary: After the synagogue service, many Jews and devout proselytes follow Paul and Barnabas, who urge them 'to continue in the grace of God' (prosmenein te chariti tou theou).
sections.relevance: The verb prosmenein ('to remain in, to continue in, to abide in') presupposes that remaining in God's grace is not automatic. The neutral reading notes that 'the exhortation to continue assumes that the response of faith is not a one-time event but an ongoing posture. Grace has been extended; they must remain in it.' This is the same verb (prosmenein) used in Acts 11:23, where Barnabas urges the Antioch believers to remain true to the Lord. The consistent use of this verb for exhorting believers to persist in what they have received implies that persistence is both necessary and not guaranteed.
key_phrases: urged them to continue in the grace of God

sections.section_title: Jewish Jealousy and the Turn to the Gentiles
sections.summary: When almost the whole city gathers the next Sabbath, the Jews are filled with jealousy and contradict Paul; Paul declares 'Since you thrust it aside and judge yourselves unworthy of eternal life, behold, we are turning to the Gentiles,' grounding this turn in Isaiah 49:6.
sections.relevance: The phrase 'you judge yourselves unworthy of eternal life' uses active, reflexive verbs -- the rejection is self-determined, not divinely imposed. The neutral reading emphasizes the deliberate contrast: 'No one has judged them unworthy. God has not excluded them. They have excluded themselves.' While this describes the initial rejection of the gospel rather than a believer losing standing, it establishes the principle that human response determines one's relationship to eternal life. Eternal life is available, but human beings can exclude themselves from it by their own choices.
key_phrases: judge yourselves unworthy of eternal life

sections.section_title: The Response of the Gentiles -- Appointed to Eternal Life
sections.summary: The Gentiles rejoice and glorify the word of the Lord, and 'as many as were appointed to eternal life believed' -- using the passive voice (tetagmenoi, from tasso) to describe their reception in contrast to the active verbs of Jewish self-exclusion.
sections.relevance: The neutral reading identifies a 'deliberate asymmetry' between v. 46 (active, reflexive verbs for rejection) and v. 48 (passive verb for reception): 'rejection is described with active verbs (human choice), reception corresponds to a divine arrangement.' The passive participle tetagmenoi ('having been appointed/arranged/enrolled') indicates that the Gentiles' reception of eternal life corresponds to a prior divine ordering. If God has appointed people to eternal life, this could imply that what God has arranged is not contingent on fluctuating human performance. However, the neutral reading carefully notes that the author 'does not elaborate on the mechanism or timing of the appointment' and is narrating what happened rather than constructing a theory about the relationship between divine appointment and human response.
key_phrases: as many as were appointed to eternal life believed

sections.section_title: The Word Spreads, Persecution Comes, Joy Remains
sections.summary: The word of the Lord spreads throughout the region; the Jews incite persecution that drives Paul and Barnabas from the district; the new disciples left behind are filled with joy and with the Holy Spirit.
